Inner Monologue is a training and inference procedure in Moshi that jointly models text and audio tokens, allowing the model to fully exploit the knowledge imparted from the text modality while remaining a speech‑to‑speech system. [1][2] It decomposes speech into a chain of text, semantic and acoustic tokens and predicts this structured sequence in a hierarchical manner, enabling the model to represent all utterances as both text and speech rather than switching between modalities. [1] Because the acoustic tokens are integrated into the same generative model, Moshi can generate arbitrary voices and conditions instead of being limited to a single speaker. [1] The hierarchical modeling allows decomposing the generation task without increasing the sequence length of the Transformer outputs, and the per‑frame decomposition means each prediction step outputs a speech frame, making Moshi compatible with real‑time generation. [1] Finally, when combined with a delay between token types, Inner Monologue enables deriving streaming TTS and ASR systems from Moshi, supporting full‑duplex spoken dialogue. [1]

H‑Net’s encoder and decoder networks are built from Mamba‑2 layers, a type of state‑space model (SSM) [1]. These layers are chosen because they handle fine‑grained, uncompressed sequences efficiently and provide a strong inductive bias for compression, which helps build abstractions [1]. The use of SSM‑based encoders/decoders also yields higher performance than Transformer layers on both byte‑level and coarser inputs, as shown by ablation studies [1].
H‑Net’s advantage over tokenized models is greatest at the XL scale, where it outperforms the Transformer baseline by 2.6 % in zero‑shot downstream performance. [1]

The smoothing module transforms the discrete chunking operation into a continuous, differentiable one by applying an exponential moving average (EMA) that blends the current compressed representation with the previous one weighted by the boundary confidence score [𝑃𝑡] [1]. This allows gradients to flow through chunk boundaries during training without stochastic exploration, preserving autoregressive causality because each smoothed output depends only on past compressed representations [2]. When the boundary confidence is high (𝑃𝑡 ≈ 1.0) the EMA preserves the discrete boundary (¯𝑧𝑡 ≈ 𝑧𝑡), whereas low‑confidence boundaries (𝑃𝑡 ≈ 0.5) are smoothed with information from earlier chunks, providing an adaptive error‑correction mechanism [1]. By smoothly interpolating between discrete choices based on confidence, the module also stabilizes training and prevents overfitting to suboptimal chunking patterns early in training [1].
